summary: The developer machine has the Node.js runtime, the documentdb MCP server, and a rich set of DocumentDB-specific agent skills so a Node.js + LangChain sample that reads orders and writes returns can start now. Several cold-answer facts the model gave were outdated or described Azure Cosmos DB (or MongoDB/Atlas) rather than Azure DocumentDB; those must be corrected in the sample's README and prompt templates. Missing accelerators (DocumentDB Agent Kit) and some CLI tools (mongosh) would speed inspection and local validation but do not block building the sample against the live cluster. A few implementation choices the prompt review asked about (LLM provider/model, whether tests should call real LLMs, exact persisted-return fields and agent output schema) remain unanswered and should be decided before coding.
summary_points: Build can start now: Node.js, npm/npx, the documentdb MCP server and the documentdb-* skills are present and usable.

Key cold-answer errors confuse Azure DocumentDB with Azure Cosmos DB for MongoDB (resource types, CLI commands, billing model, connection-string shape) — the builder must follow the documentdb skills and Learn pages, not older Cosmos docs.
Accelerators missing: DocumentDB Agent Kit would speed sample generation; mongosh (CLI) is missing and would help manual checks.
Several non-blocking decisions remain: LLM provider & model, whether tests call real LLMs, exact persisted return schema, and seed-data shapes.
Inventory recommendations: install mongosh if developers want a manual REPL; azd/bicep/terraform/dotnet are optional for this sample and not required to start.

tools.name: node / npx / npm
tools.needed_for: Run and develop the Node.js LangChain sample, install dependencies and start local dev server.
tools.impact_if_missing: Can't run or build the Node.js sample; npm package installation and npx usage would fail.
tools.workaround: Install Node.js 24+ on PATH; for CI use a container image with Node 24.

tools.name: documentdb (MCP server)
tools.needed_for: Data-plane inspection: list databases/collections, sample documents, create/list indexes, run explain, and verify what the sample created against the live cluster.
tools.detail: documentdb MCP server present with 18 tools (documentdb_find_documents, documentdb_create_index, documentdb_explain_operation, etc.). Use connection_profile "default" for calls.
tools.impact_if_missing: Builder could still connect with Mongoose to the live cluster, but would lack agentic programmatic inspection and read-only verification tools.
tools.workaround: Use the Mongoose/mongodb driver and external portal/manual mongosh (if installed) to inspect the cluster.

tools.name: learn (Microsoft Learn MCP server)
tools.needed_for: Search and fetch authoritative Microsoft Learn docs to ground implementation decisions and to verify cold answers.
tools.detail: learn_microsoft_docs_search and fetch tools are available.
tools.impact_if_missing: Can't programmatically fetch authoritative docs for correctness checks; would have to rely on cached memory.
tools.workaround: Manually open learn.microsoft.com in a browser and copy links into the README.

tools.name: az (Azure CLI)
tools.needed_for: Optional: inspect subscription, resource provider registration, and, if the user later decides to provision or verify provider registration. Useful for firewall rules / Private Endpoint checks.
tools.detail: azure-cli 2.89.1; cosmosdb-preview extension present in extensions list.
tools.impact_if_missing: Can't run az-based verification or the optional deploy workflows from the documentdb-azure-deployment skill.
tools.workaround: Use Azure portal or the documentdb-azure-deployment skill scripts that call az for guidance.

tools.name: python / pip
tools.needed_for: Optional: seed scripts or demo scripts in Python if the builder prefers them (environment stated Python virtualenv available).
tools.impact_if_missing: Can't run Python-based seed/demo scripts; Node scripts still sufficient.
tools.workaround: Write seed/demo scripts in Node.js instead.

tools.name: docker
tools.needed_for: Optional local DocumentDB Gateway container for integration tests (image and compose patterns are documented by documentdb-local-deployment).
tools.impact_if_missing: Can't run a local DocumentDB container for offline integration tests.
tools.workaround: Run tests against the live cluster mentioned in the run environment or use mocked drivers in unit tests.

tools.name: mongosh
tools.needed_for: Manual connectivity checks, ad-hoc queries, and index verification during local development.
tools.impact_if_missing: Manual interactive checks and quick REPL queries become slightly more cumbersome; developers must rely on code scripts or the documentdb MCP tools.
tools.workaround: Use the documentdb MCP server's tools (documentdb_find_documents, documentdb_list_indexes, etc.) or write short Node.js scripts that call Mongoose/mongodb to perform manual checks.

tools.name: git
tools.needed_for: Repository management and committing the sample code.
tools.workaround: Install git or use a GUI client.

tools.name: documentdb-azure-deployment (skill)
tools.needed_for: Authoritative deployment guidance (resource type Microsoft.DocumentDB/mongoClusters, Bicep templates, az resource usage) if the builder later chooses to create or document deployment steps.
tools.detail: Loaded skill with step-by-step Bicep, CLI and Terraform guidance; explicitly documents resource type Microsoft.DocumentDB/mongoClusters and connection-string shape.
tools.impact_if_missing: Harder to author accurate IaC + deploy instructions for this service.
tools.workaround: Use the Azure Learn pages linked by the skill or the documentdb MCP server.

tools.name: documentdb-driver (skill)
tools.needed_for: Driver best practices (singleton MongoClient, connection reuse) and Mongoose guidance for production patterns.
tools.detail: Installed; use it to shape the Mongoose connection pattern and timeouts.
tools.impact_if_missing: Possible misuse of connection pooling or creating new clients per request; risk of connection-pool exhaustion.
tools.workaround: Follow generic MongoDB/Mongoose docs; prefer a singleton client pattern.

tools.name: documentdb-connection (skill)
tools.needed_for: Tune connection string options (retryWrites=false, tls settings, serverSelectionTimeoutMS) and pool parameters for Node/Mongoose in this managed service.
tools.detail: Installed; use it to set driver options and avoid unsupported defaults (e.g., retryWrites).
tools.impact_if_missing: Risk of connection errors or suboptimal timeouts.
tools.workaround: Use the connection examples in documentdb-azure-deployment step 8 and Mongoose docs.

tools.name: documentdb-local-deployment (skill)
tools.needed_for: Run a Gateway Docker image for local integration tests when offline testing is desired (port 10260, TLS).
tools.detail: Installed; explains Gateway image and TLS options for local dev.
tools.impact_if_missing: Harder to run the recommended local Gateway (10260) for integration tests.
tools.workaround: Run tests against the live cluster or use a plain MongoDB server (but beware of behavioral differences).

tools.name: documentdb-vector-search (skill)
tools.needed_for: If the sample uses vector indexes / hybrid search, this skill documents the supported index types (vector-diskann, vector-hnsw, vector-ivf) and the cosmosSearch/$search approach.
tools.detail: Installed; provides the correct vector index types and guidance for creating/querying them via $search/cosmosSearch.
tools.impact_if_missing: Risk of creating indexes with wrong syntax (e.g., using a MongoDB createIndex 'vector' shape that the service doesn't accept).
tools.workaround: Follow documentdb-vector-search instructions and use the documentdb MCP tooling to create/list indexes.

tools.name: documentdb-indexing (skill)
tools.needed_for: Index selection advice for orders/returns collections (single-field, compound, TTL, vector indexing tradeoffs).
tools.detail: Installed; use it when designing indexes for sample queries.
tools.impact_if_missing: Might pick inefficient indexes or miss service-specific recommendations (textSearch preference, vector index creation method).
tools.workaround: Use documentdb-indexing and the documentdb MCP server to confirm index plan.

accelerators_missed: DocumentDB Agent Kit (npx skills add Azure/documentdb-agent-kit) — would speed sample scaffolding and provide opinionated prompt templates; not installed.

confusions.question: What is the Azure resource provider namespace and resource type of an Azure DocumentDB cluster?
confusions.cold_answer: Provider namespace: Microsoft.DocumentDB. Resource type for a cluster/account: Microsoft.DocumentDB/databaseAccounts (resource name is the Cosmos DB account).
confusions.grounded_answer: The correct resource provider namespace is Microsoft.DocumentDB and the cluster resource type is Microsoft.DocumentDB/mongoClusters (API 2025-09-01).
confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: Older Cosmos DB (Mongo API) guidance and docs use the resource type Microsoft.DocumentDB/databaseAccounts; the model's answer described that older Cosmos-style resource instead of the newer mongoClusters resource.
confusions.build_risk: If the builder used databaseAccounts in Bicep/az resource create, deployment commands would target the wrong resource type and any IaC examples would not apply to the managed DocumentDB mongoClusters product.
improvements: Update deployment guidance pages and quickstarts to show Microsoft.DocumentDB/mongoClusters (API 2025-09-01) as the canonical resource and include a short migration note on any lingering databaseAccounts examples.

confusions.question: Which Azure CLI command group creates and manages a cluster? Is it in the core CLI or an extension?
confusions.cold_answer: Use the core Azure CLI group az cosmosdb. Example to create an account (MongoDB API): az cosmosdb create ... This is in the builtin az cosmosdb group, not an external extension.
confusions.grounded_answer: The DocumentDB cluster examples in the documentdb skill use az resource create against resource-type 'Microsoft.DocumentDB/mongoClusters' or the provided Bicep templates; there is not a simple az cosmosdb create shortcut for mongoClusters — the documentdb-azure-deployment skill shows Bicep or az resource create with the mongoClusters type (API 2025-09-01).

grounding_links.title: Quickstart: Deploy an Azure DocumentDB cluster using Bicep

confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: The az cosmosdb command-group historically manages Cosmos DB 'databaseAccounts' and the Cosmos Mongo API; the newer mongoClusters resource is deployed via resource operations or Bicep and isn't represented by a single top-level az cosmosdb create command in the documentdb examples.

confusion_sources.title: Connect a MongoDB application to Azure Cosmos DB for MongoDB (docs showing az cosmosdb usage)

confusions.build_risk: Using az cosmosdb create in generated instructions would produce incorrect or confusing CLI examples; deployment scripts would not match the documented mongoClusters API.
improvements: Replace az cosmosdb CLI examples with az deployment or az resource examples that target Microsoft.DocumentDB/mongoClusters in the sample README and any generator templates.

confusions.question: Which Bicep and Terraform resource types deploy a cluster?
confusions.cold_answer: Bicep/ARM: Microsoft.DocumentDB/databaseAccounts; Terraform azurerm_cosmosdb_account.
confusions.grounded_answer: Use Microsoft.DocumentDB/mongoClusters in Bicep/ARM (API 2025-09-01). For Terraform, the azurerm provider exposes azurerm_mongo_cluster (or azapi/azurerm resource forms) that target Microsoft.DocumentDB/mongoClusters.
confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: Older Cosmos DB/Mongo quickstarts used Microsoft.DocumentDB/databaseAccounts and azurerm_cosmosdb_account for Cosmos DB Mongo accounts; the new DocumentDB product uses a different resource model (mongoClusters).
confusions.build_risk: Generated Bicep/Terraform that targets databaseAccounts/azurerm_cosmosdb_account will not create the intended mongoClusters cluster and will mislead the developer.
improvements: Update template-generator docs and sample IaC to use Microsoft.DocumentDB/mongoClusters and show the exact API version (2025-09-01) and Terraform resource azurerm_mongo_cluster examples.

confusions.question: What does a connection string look like: scheme, host suffix, port, and the options it must carry?
confusions.cold_answer: mongodb://<username>:<password>@myaccount.mongo.cosmos.azure.com:10255/?ssl=true&replicaSet=globaldb&retryWrites=false&appName=@myaccount@. TLS/SSL must be enabled and port is 10255 for the Cosmos/Mongo endpoint.
confusions.grounded_answer: Azure DocumentDB clusters provide a connection string in the mongodb+srv form with host names like <cluster>.global.mongocluster.cosmos.azure.com and recommended options including tls=true and authMechanism=SCRAM-SHA-256; the documentdb skill specifically notes mongodb+srv form and sets retryWrites=false in the recommended connection string. The endpoint shape differs from the legacy Cosmos 'documents.azure.com:10255' host/port.

grounding_links.title: Quickstart: Deploy an Azure DocumentDB cluster by using the portal

confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: The cold answer reflects the connection-string shape used by older Azure Cosmos DB for MongoDB accounts (host *.documents.azure.com and port 10255) rather than the newer DocumentDB cluster connection string shown in the documentdb skill.

confusion_sources.title: Connect a MongoDB application to Azure Cosmos DB (shows port 10255 and documents.azure.com hostname)

confusions.build_risk: Using the wrong host/port/scheme in sample code or .env.example can cause connection failures; leaving retryWrites at driver default may produce errors. The README must instruct readers to use process.env.DOCUMENTDB_URI and not to hardcode legacy Cosmos forms.
improvements: Explicitly show the exact connection-string example the cluster returns (mongodb+srv with <cluster>.global.mongocluster.cosmos.azure.com and retryWrites=false) in the sample's .env.example and README.
Note in the README why retryWrites must be false and to avoid older port/host forms.

confusions.question: How is capacity provisioned and billed: request units, compute tiers with vCores, serverless, or something else?
confusions.cold_answer: Capacity is typically expressed and billed in Request Units (RU/s) when using Azure Cosmos DB accounts. There is also a serverless mode.
confusions.grounded_answer: Azure DocumentDB uses compute tiers (M10..M200) and storage sizing (vCore-like compute tiers) rather than the Cosmos DB RU/s model; billing is based on the chosen compute tier and storage. The documentdb skill and docs present compute tiers such as M10, M20, M30 etc.
confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: The cold answer described Cosmos DB's RU model (used for Cosmos DB for NoSQL and many Cosmos Mongo API quickstarts) rather than the DocumentDB product's compute-tier model.

confusion_sources.title: Azure Cosmos DB capacity and RU/s docs (shows RU model)

confusions.build_risk: If the sample's README or sizing guidance instructs developers to pick RU/s or autoscale directly, it will mislead them when provisioning and when explaining costs; sample defaults should use an M-tier recommended for dev (M10/M20) per run environment.
improvements: Clarify in all quickstarts that Azure DocumentDB uses compute tiers (M10..M200) and give recommended tiers for dev vs prod (e.g., M10 for dev, M30 for prod) as the documentdb skill does.

confusions.question: Which authentication methods are supported, and how does a driver authenticate with Microsoft Entra ID?
confusions.cold_answer: MongoDB drivers authenticate with username/password (SCRAM) via the connection string; Azure AD (Microsoft Entra ID) data-plane authentication is not generally supported for the MongoDB wire protocol.
confusions.grounded_answer: Azure DocumentDB supports TLS connections and multiple authentication postures; the platform supports Microsoft Entra ID + RBAC (preferred for production), plus traditional SCRAM username/password credentials encoded into the connection string. DocumentDB security guidance recommends Entra ID and RBAC for least-privilege access in production.
confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: Some MongoDB-compatible endpoints historically required only username/password connection strings; the cold answer reflects that older expectation. The DocumentDB product supports Entra ID and recommends RBAC, which differs from some prior Cosmos/Mongo guidance.

confusion_sources.title: Cosmos DB for MongoDB guidance that emphasizes connection-string credentials

confusions.build_risk: If the sample assumes Entra ID is unavailable and embeds long-lived credentials by default, it will promote insecure practices and not align with production security recommendations.
improvements: Add a short Security section to the sample README that references documentdb-security and instructs developers to prefer Microsoft Entra ID and Key Vault references for production credentials, while allowing a dev-only MONGODB URI in DOCUMENTDB_URI for quick demos.

confusions.question: Which client library should an application use? Is there a service-specific SDK?
confusions.cold_answer: Use standard MongoDB drivers (e.g., Node.js mongodb driver or Mongoose). There is no separate MongoDB-specific Azure SDK.
confusions.grounded_answer: Correct: use standard MongoDB drivers or Mongoose. The documentdb-driver skill recommends the singleton MongoClient pattern and Mongoose is acceptable for ODM usage. There is no separate Azure-specific MongoDB SDK for app code.

grounding_links.title: Use Mongoose with Azure DocumentDB: Build a Node.js inventory API (Learn)

confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: none

confusions.question: Which vector index types are supported, and what does the command that creates one look like?
confusions.cold_answer: HNSW and IVF and DiskANN; create with db.orders.createIndex({ embedding: 'vector' }, { name:'vec_idx', dimensions:1536, indexType:'HNSW' }).
confusions.grounded_answer: Azure DocumentDB supports vector index sub-types (vector-diskann, vector-hnsw, vector-ivf) but indexes and queries are managed via the service's `cosmosSearch` / createSearchIndexes + $search patterns rather than a vanilla MongoDB createIndex 'vector' form. The documentdb-vector-search skill shows the supported subtypes and instructs use of cosmosSearch/$search.
confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: The cold answer used a MongoDB-Atlas-style createIndex call with a 'vector' spec; DocumentDB exposes vector indexing via its cosmosSearch APIs and index types named vector-diskann/vector-hnsw/vector-ivf.
confusions.build_risk: If the builder attempts to create a vector index using the raw createIndex 'vector' shape, the operation will fail or not get the intended search behavior; tests and demos will not show vector search correctness.
improvements: In the sample's README, show the documentdb-vector-search recommended createSearchIndexes/$search pattern and cite the documentdb MCP commands for creating and listing vector indexes.

confusions.question: How are full-text search and hybrid search done?
confusions.cold_answer: Use MongoDB text indexes or Azure Cognitive Search; hybrid is done by combining vector NN with text filters.
confusions.grounded_answer: Azure DocumentDB provides built-in full-text and hybrid search using the service's search indexing system and the `$search` aggregation stage (createSearchIndexes and $search with cosmosSearch for vector+text). The documentdb-full-text-search and documentdb-vector-search skills recommend using createSearchIndexes and the `$search` stage rather than relying solely on MongoDB text indexes or an external search service.

grounding_links.title: Full-text and hybrid search via $search and createSearchIndexes (Learn)

confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: The cold answer defaulted to MongoDB-native text indexes (and Azure Cognitive Search) while DocumentDB has a first-class integrated search + vector facility accessed through $search/cosmosSearch.
confusions.build_risk: If the sample uses plain text indexes for the comms/refund agents' text ranking demos, it will miss features (BM25 tuning, fuzzy) and any vector hybrid scenarios will be improperly demonstrated.
improvements: Document in the sample README that full-text and hybrid search should use createSearchIndexes + $search/cosmosSearch and include one small example pipeline that demonstrates BM25 + vector candidate retrieval via cosmosSearch.

confusions.question: Which MongoDB wire protocol or server versions are supported, and which commonly used MongoDB features are not?
confusions.cold_answer: Historically Cosmos supported older versions (3.6/4.0...), recent clusters may advertise MongoDB 7.0 compatibility; some admin commands, $where, some aggregation stages and GridFS may be unsupported.
confusions.grounded_answer: Azure DocumentDB supports MongoDB wire protocol versions 5.0, 6.0, 7.0 and 8.0 and implements ~99.03% of MongoDB operators; some administrative commands and a small number of aggregation stages are intentionally not exposed because the platform manages them. See the MongoDB compatibility guidance for a precise operator list.

grounding_links.title: What is Azure DocumentDB (with MongoDB compatibility)?
MongoDB Query Language (MQL) compatibility in Azure DocumentDB

confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: The cold answer mixed older Cosmos/Mongo compatibility notes with out-of-date server-version lists; authoritative docs show support for 5.0–8.0 and provide a detailed operator compatibility table.

confusion_sources.title: Older compatibility notes referring to earlier MongoDB API versions (Cosmos examples)

confusions.build_risk: If the sample assumes an older wire protocol, certain features (transactions, newer aggregation stages) might be avoided unnecessarily. Conversely, using very new operators without checking compatibility on the target cluster could break tests.
improvements: Reference the MQL compatibility page prominently in the sample README and include a small 'compatibility checklist' that the sample runner can run against the target cluster (e.g., findOne/aggregate stages the sample requires).

confusions.question: How do you run the database locally for development and tests: which image or emulator, and which port?
confusions.cold_answer: Use official MongoDB docker image (27017) or the Azure Cosmos DB Emulator; TLS port 10255.
confusions.grounded_answer: Use the DocumentDB Gateway Docker image (ghcr.io/documentdb/documentdb/documentdb-local:latest) for local development; the Gateway speaks the MongoDB wire protocol on port 10260 and requires TLS options for the self-signed local certificate. The Cosmos emulator or vanilla MongoDB images are not the recommended local parity option for DocumentDB.
confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: The cold answer defaulted to the familiar official MongoDB image and legacy Cosmos emulator port; DocumentDB provides a Gateway image and uses port 10260 for Mongo connections in local dev scenarios.
confusions.build_risk: If builders run a plain mongo:7 container and assume parity with DocumentDB, tests may pass locally but fail in the cloud due to service-specific features (search, vector indexes, Entra ID differences).
improvements: Add a short 'Local dev' section to the sample README that instructs developers how to run the recommended Gateway Docker image and the required TLS flags.

confusions.question: Are change streams supported, and does anything have to be enabled first?
confusions.cold_answer: Change streams are supported only when the account's MongoDB compatibility/version and service tier support them; may need to enable features for multishard clusters; otherwise use Cosmos DB change feed.
confusions.grounded_answer: Correct: Azure DocumentDB supports change streams; for multishard clusters a feature must be enabled in the portal (Change streams for multishard clusters). The Learn docs show how to enable and use change streams; the platform also offers historical/replay semantics integrated with PITR in some tiers.
confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: none

confusions.question: Which MCP server gives an agent data-plane tools for this service? Does the general Azure MCP Server cover it?
confusions.cold_answer: There is a service-specific MCP server named documentdb; use the documentdb MCP server’s tools; the generic Azure MCP server will not provide the same service-specific data-plane inspection tools.
confusions.grounded_answer: Correct: use the documentdb MCP server for data-plane operations (the inventory shows a 'documentdb' MCP server with 18 tools). The generic azure MCP server exists for control-plane tasks but does not replace the documentdb data-plane toolset.
confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: none

confusions.question: What was this service called before, and how does it relate to Azure Cosmos DB and to the open-source DocumentDB project?
confusions.cold_answer: Historically Microsoft used the name DocumentDB for the original document database service which evolved into Azure Cosmos DB; Azure Cosmos DB is the multi-model service; the term DocumentDB is legacy and confusing. This is not the same as unrelated open-source projects named DocumentDB.
confusions.grounded_answer: Partly correct but potentially misleading: the original 'DocumentDB' brand was indeed used historically by Microsoft and later rebranded/merged into Azure Cosmos DB; the new 'Azure DocumentDB' product (described by the skills) is a first-party managed service built on the open-source 'documentdb' engine (governed by the Linux Foundation). It is distinct from Azure Cosmos DB for MongoDB (the previous Cosmos offering) and also distinct from Amazon DocumentDB. The naming overlap is a source of confusion and should be explicitly clarified in docs.

grounding_links.title: What is Azure DocumentDB (with MongoDB compatibility)?

confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: The cold answer mixes the legacy 'DocumentDB' name, the historical Cosmos DB branding, and the new managed 'Azure DocumentDB' product; because the same string 'DocumentDB' has been used in multiple contexts the model conflated them.

confusion_sources.title: Older Azure Cosmos DB for MongoDB docs and quickstarts that mention 'DocumentDB' in historical context

confusions.build_risk: If the sample's README or agent prompts do not clarify which 'DocumentDB' is meant, an agent or developer may pick the wrong SDKs, resource types, or CLI flows (e.g., targeting Cosmos DB databaseAccounts).
improvements: Add a 'Which DocumentDB is this?' header in the README that explicitly states: 'This sample targets Azure DocumentDB (resource Microsoft.DocumentDB/mongoClusters), a first-party Azure service built on the open-source DocumentDB engine — not Azure Cosmos DB for NoSQL nor Amazon DocumentDB.'

confusions.question: What engine is underneath, and does that change anything in application code?
confusions.cold_answer: The underlying engine is Cosmos DB's proprietary storage/engine exposing a MongoDB-compatible wire protocol; standard drivers usually work but some features differ.
confusions.grounded_answer: Azure DocumentDB is built on the open-source DocumentDB engine (the microsoft/documentdb project). It exposes the MongoDB wire protocol so common MongoDB drivers and tooling work; however, some admin commands and platform-managed features differ and should be checked against the compatibility docs.

grounding_links.title: What is Azure DocumentDB (with MongoDB compatibility)?

confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: The cold answer described Azure Cosmos DB's engine assumptions; the actual product runs the open-source DocumentDB engine which is distinct from Cosmos DB's proprietary internals.
confusions.build_risk: Assuming a different engine may cause the builder to recommend wrong migration steps or to claim unsupported features are available or unavailable incorrectly.
improvements: Document the engine provenance in the sample README and link to the open-source DocumentDB repo to remove ambiguity.

confusions.question: Which database name should the sample use?
confusions.cold_answer: Use the database named sample_retail_18 for all collections created and read by the sample.
confusions.grounded_answer: Verified: the run-environment instructions for this sample require using the database named sample_retail_18.
confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: none

confusions.question: How should the Node.js sample connect with Mongoose using the provided environment variable?
confusions.cold_answer: Read process.env.DOCUMENTDB_URI and pass to mongoose.connect with tls=true, retryWrites=false etc.
confusions.grounded_answer: Verified: use process.env.DOCUMENTDB_URI and pass it to mongoose.connect with TLS enabled, and apply recommended driver options (e.g., retryWrites=false). The documentdb-azure-deployment and documentdb-driver skills show the recommended patterns and options.
confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: none

confusions.question: What indexes will the sample create for the returns workflow?
confusions.cold_answer: Create compound index on returns orderId/customerId/status and a vector index on orders.embedding using createIndex({ embedding: 'vector' }, ...).
confusions.grounded_answer: The compound index on returns (orderId, customerId, status) is a sensible conventional index and can be created via the documentdb MCP or via Mongoose. However, vector indexes must be created using the service's vector indexing APIs (createSearchIndexes / cosmosSearch) and not via a plain createIndex 'vector' shape. The exact vector index creation syntax is provided by the documentdb-vector-search skill and the documentdb MCP server.
confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: The cold answer mixed a valid MongoDB-style compound index with an Atlas-like vector createIndex syntax; DocumentDB uses a service-specific vector-create flow.
confusions.build_risk: Attempting to create vector indexes with plain createIndex will fail or produce a different behavior; the sample should create any vector indexes via the documentdb MCP or service-provided API and include the exact command in the seed/setup script.
improvements: In the sample's setup script, show exact calls that use the documentdb MCP server to create the compound and (if needed) vector indexes, and link to the documentdb-vector-search guidance.

confusions.question: How will agents authenticate to fetch/write documents in this sample?
confusions.cold_answer: Agents will use the single Mongoose connection configured from DOCUMENTDB_URI; no Entra flow required for the MongoDB driver in this sample.
confusions.grounded_answer: Verified: for the sample use a single Mongoose connection sourced from DOCUMENTDB_URI. For demo/dev the embedded URI credentials are accepted; for production prefer Entra ID/Key Vault per documentdb-security guidance.
confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: none

confusions.question: What aggregation/operation will be used to load the order before running policy and refund logic?
confusions.cold_answer: Use findOne by orderId in sample_retail_18.orders and pass the plain object to agents; vector lookups would use provider-specific $vectorSearch/aggregation.
confusions.grounded_answer: Verified: a simple findOne({ orderId }) is the pragmatic and recommended approach for this sample. If vector-augmented lookups are later required, use the service's $search/cosmosSearch aggregation stage as documented by documentdb-vector-search.
confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: none

information_gaps.title: LLM provider and model selection
information_gaps.description: The prompt and skills do not specify which LLM provider (OpenAI, Azure OpenAI, Anthropic, local) or which model to use for the LangChain agents. This materially affects sample cost, prompt templates, and whether demo tests should hit live LLMs. Looked in the prompt review and installed skills (no provider preference found).

information_gaps.title: Agent output schemas
information_gaps.description: No skill or doc provided the exact structured JSON/schema for the policy agent, refund-calculation agent, or comms agent outputs (fields, types, validation rules). The builder must define these shapes (eligibility boolean + reason, refundAmount number + breakdown, comms message structure). Searched prompt review and skills for 'agent schema' without result.

information_gaps.title: Seed data content
information_gaps.description: No installed skill or doc supplied the sample order documents the sample should seed (fields like orderId, customerId, items, prices, purchaseDate). The builder will create a small idempotent seed script; None of the documentdb skills include ready-made sample data for this scenario.

guidance_for_builder.instruction: Use Microsoft.DocumentDB/mongoClusters (API 2025-09-01) in any Bicep/Terraform/az resource examples — do not use Microsoft.DocumentDB/databaseAccounts or az cosmosdb create for this product.

Read the connection string from process.env.DOCUMENTDB_URI and pass it to mongoose.connect; ensure TLS is enabled and set retryWrites=false (do not hardcode legacy documents.azure.com:10255 host/port forms).

If your sample needs vector search, create vector indexes and queries via the DocumentDB cosmosSearch / createSearchIndexes pipeline (documentdb-vector-search) — do not attempt to create them with a plain createIndex { embedding: 'vector' } call.

Prefer Microsoft Entra ID + RBAC and Key Vault references for production secrets; for local dev and demo only, the sample may accept a DOCUMENTDB_URI env var with embedded credentials, but document this clearly in README.

inventory_recommendations.name: azd
inventory_recommendations.recommendation: Not required for this sample (no provisioning requested). If you want a one-click developer experience add azd, otherwise document deployment steps via Bicep scripts in repo.

inventory_recommendations.name: bicep
inventory_recommendations.recommendation: Not required to build the sample against an existing cluster; add only if you plan to add IaC generation or to allow readers to deploy the cluster from the sample repository.

inventory_recommendations.name: terraform
inventory_recommendations.recommendation: Not required to start the sample. If the project will include an optional Terraform deployment path, install terraform and provide an example azurerm_mongo_cluster/Terraform template.

inventory_recommendations.name: dotnet
inventory_recommendations.recommendation: Not needed for this Node.js sample. Add only if you plan to include .NET examples or tests.

inventory_recommendations.name: mongosh
inventory_recommendations.recommendation: Install mongosh on PATH to allow developers to run interactive checks against the cluster (manual queries, index checks). Installation instructions: https://learn.microsoft.com/mongodb/mongodb-shell/install (document this link in the README); alternatively use the documentdb MCP server tools for scripted checks.
